items.title: Flechette’s momentum and Arrow JS friction point to a real split in the JavaScript data stack
items.why_now: This week produced a cleaner JS-data-stack story than another maintenance note. `uwdata/flechette` shipped `v2.4.0` on Apr 10 while continuing to position itself as a faster, lighter, zero-dependency alternative to Arrow JS. At the same time, fresh `apache/arrow-js` issues from a DuckDB-WASM frontend consumer exposed product-level gaps that matter in real browser data apps: no extension-type registry, which forces every consumer to hand-decode DuckDB Arrow extensions, and silent `Date32` precision loss for wide date ranges. The Kenny-fit angle is not “library drama.” It is that the JavaScript data stack is now mature enough for a real implementation split: the reference library is no longer automatically the best fit once bundle size, frontend correctness, and browser-consumer ergonomics start to dominate.
questions: Do you think the JS data ecosystem is entering the phase where “reference implementation” and “best production library” naturally diverge?
Where do browser-native consumers feel Arrow JS pain first in practice: extension types, bundle size, extraction speed, type correctness, or something else?
Is the sharper public framing here about Arrow specifically, or about the broader fact that JavaScript data tooling is developing its own priorities instead of inheriting backend assumptions?

items.title: Golden Analytics is a clean founder case for rebuilding BI around AI-native workflows instead of bolting AI onto the old stack
items.why_now: Golden Analytics launched from Seattle on Apr 7 with $7M in seed funding and a founder who has seen two prior BI platform shifts from the inside. François Ajenstat’s framing is unusually crisp: Tableau, Power BI, and Looker are strong products, but they are “bolting on AI” instead of being built around it from the start. The demo details make this more than generic launch copy: a web-based BI product with a “slider of autonomy,” orchestration across multiple specialist models, and a deliberate rejection of the chatbot-as-analyst replacement framing. It also intersects cleanly with Kenny’s world because Golden says it was built heavily with AI coding tools and is treating AI as the new workflow/control surface, not as one more feature checkbox. The founder lesson is that category resets are real when the core interaction model changes, and incumbents often carry too much product and architecture debt to make that turn cleanly.
questions: What kinds of product categories actually deserve an AI-native rebuild, versus a disciplined AI add-on to an existing workflow?
When does “AI-native” describe a genuine control-surface shift rather than just better launch copy?

Do you buy the founder claim that incumbents are structurally bad at this kind of reset, or is the harder truth that most startups still underestimate how much trust and workflow design the old tools already earned?

items.title: Squirreling’s latest optimizer burst makes browser-native SQL look less like a demo and more like a real analytical engine
items.why_now: `squirreling` had a concentrated Apr 12 push that is more meaningful than routine maintenance: correlated subqueries landed, a TopN node was added to cut `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` memory usage, and projection pushdown through `UNION ALL` was added specifically to avoid out-of-memory failures on wide rows and large JSON/message columns across shards. The Kenny-fit angle is not “look, another release.” It is that browser-native SQL engines are starting to pick up the kinds of optimizer and memory-behavior work that make people trust them for real exploratory analysis instead of toy demos. That creates a cleaner Pillar 2/3 story about what has to become true for pure-JS browser data tooling to feel production-grade: not just parsing files, but surviving realistic query shapes and ugly wide data under browser constraints.
questions: What are the specific query patterns or memory pathologies that separate a browser SQL demo from an engine you actually trust on messy data?
Is the sharper framing here about browser-native maturity, or about the fact that database-history problems are now replaying inside the browser under tighter startup and memory limits?
Where do you think pure-JS query engines still hit real walls compared with DuckDB-WASM or server-side systems?

items.title: Berkeley’s benchmark-exploit paper is a reminder that AI coding leaderboards are easy to optimize against and hard to trust
items.why_now: UC Berkeley researchers published a fresh April 2026 teardown showing an exploit agent could achieve near-perfect scores across eight major agent benchmarks — including SWE-bench, WebArena, OSWorld, Terminal-Bench, and GAIA — without actually solving the tasks. The concrete examples are brutal: a tiny `conftest.py` can force SWE-bench Verified to pass, a fake `curl` wrapper can perfect-score Terminal-Bench, and WebArena could leak answers through `file://` access to task config. The bigger Kenny-fit lesson is not just that benchmarks can be gamed. It is that AI engineering discourse is still too eager to treat leaderboard movement as product truth, even when the eval harness itself is not adversarially robust. That creates a strong public angle on how teams should think about model/tool selection: benchmark theater is getting cheaper, so the durable skill becomes building evals and review surfaces that are harder to spoof and closer to real work.
questions: What is the plainest way to explain the difference between a benchmark score and a trustworthy review loop for real product work?
Do you want to make this about coding-model selection specifically, or the broader problem that agent evals are becoming their own attack surface?
What kinds of evals feel hardest to game in practice: hidden tasks, production-derived datasets, human review, something else?

items.title: Cirrus Labs joining OpenAI raises a sharper OSS question than growth: what do builders owe users when the business changes underneath them?
items.why_now: Cirrus Labs just announced it is joining OpenAI, shutting down Cirrus CI on June 1, stopping new Cirrus Runners customers, and relicensing source-available tools like Tart, Vetu, and Orchard under a more permissive license while dropping licensing fees. That makes this more interesting than a normal acquisition note. The founder/operator lesson is about the trust contract around open-source-adjacent developer tools: if your company changes direction, what is the right way to unwind pricing, licensing, hosted products, and user dependency without leaving everyone stranded? This feels like a real Kenny-fit Pillar 4 topic because it is not generic OSS cheerleading or GTM advice. It is a concrete case of how a tooling company behaves when the market and mission shift under it, especially in an era where agent infrastructure is pulling teams toward larger platforms.
questions: What do OSS/devtools founders actually owe users when they pivot, get acquired, or shut down a hosted product?
Is permissive relicensing the gold-standard move here, or just the least bad version of a hard transition?
Does the interesting angle live in trust, distribution, or the reality that AI-platform gravity is going to pull more small tooling companies into bigger stacks?

questions: Do you buy the idea that tiny shipped products are becoming more valuable than a polished resume for technical people?

items.title: AI coding workflows are shifting from code review toward spec, eval, and checkpoint review
items.why_now: The strongest fresh multi-source pattern this cycle was not another model/tool comparison but a workflow shift. Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report says human oversight is scaling through intelligent collaboration rather than direct line-by-line authorship. OpenAI's long-horizon Codex guidance pushes `AGENTS.md`, `plans.md`, milestone checks, and command/test evidence as the control surface for longer runs. The StrongDM "software factory" discussion is the sharpest edge of the pattern: agents write the code, run the harnesses, and humans increasingly judge scenario coverage and outcome quality instead of reading every diff. The bigger product lesson is that once agents can run for a while, the bottleneck stops being code generation and becomes whether the team has good specs, hidden evals, checkpoints, and a review surface that makes those artifacts legible.
questions: In your own workflow, where do you still read the diff carefully, and where have specs / checks / artifact review already replaced traditional code review?
If you had to name the minimal control artifacts for an AI-heavy team, what are they: AGENTS.md, plans, scenario tests, hidden evals, checkpoints, something else?
Is the sharper public framing here about how development changes, or about how review becomes the real scarce product skill?

The pattern is broader than one repo: once people run multiple coding agents, the new bottleneck becomes visibility, control surfaces, and workflow boundaries.
questions: Is the interesting founder take here that multi-agent coding immediately recreates the same review/control problem we already see in production AI products?
Which layer matters most in practice: watching what agents are doing, constraining how they interact with tools, or turning their work into something inspectable after the fact?
